matter_reference_date_basis: The candidate matter file records exam_session APRIL 2019 and matter_reference_date 2019-04. The law is stated as at April 2019; each devolution step is also checked against the date of the event it governs (1999 to 2015).
corpus_gaps: No Age of Majority Ordinance in the corpus. Amali Perera was 16 in 2005 and about 24 in 2013, so her capacity is decisive for the 2005 gift and the 2013 sale, but the only majority rule in the corpus is Civil Procedure Code s.502, which fixes majority at eighteen years expressly for the purposes of that Chapter only and cannot be relied on generally.

The Roman-Dutch rules on donation, in particular acceptance of a gift on behalf of a minor donee by a parent or guardian, are not in the corpus. Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.36 points to Roman-Dutch law but supplies no rule.

No provision in the corpus governs the reservation of a life interest or what a life tenant can pass by a later sale. The effect of the 2013 sale of Lot 1 therefore cannot be settled from statute alone.

The Married Women's Property Ordinance No. 18 of 1923 is not in the corpus. The consolidated text of Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.8 held in the corpus still requires the husband's written consent for an inter vivos disposition by a married woman and records no amendment events, so whether that requirement bound Kanthi Perera in 2005 and 2013 cannot be resolved from the corpus.

The Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 text in the corpus is the consolidated text carrying the 2022 and 2024 amendments. The 2005, 2013 and 2015 deeds were executed under earlier wording, which the corpus does not hold separately.

No provision in the corpus states whether an administrator may execute a conveyance after the testamentary proceedings have been terminated. Civil Procedure Code s.542 addresses only the reach and duration of the power of administration.

No local-authority subdivision or amalgamation approval provision was found for the 2001 amalgamation and resubdivision (Plan No. 567) in Colombo. Municipal Councils Ordinance No. 29 of 1947 as held in the corpus contains no subdivision-approval section, and Urban Development Authority Law No. 41 of 1978 mentions sub-division only in the s.29 interpretation of development.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
provisions.why_relevant: The matter concerns immovable property in Colombo devolving on two intestacies. This is the gateway provision that makes Part III of the Ordinance the governing law for that devolution.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text applies to the deaths in 2014 and to the reference date 2019-04.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the half share of Kamal De Silva on Kanthi Perera's intestacy and the half share of Anura Fernando on Amali Perera's intestacy. Both deceased left a surviving spouse.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. Applies to both deaths in 2014.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
provisions.why_relevant: Sets the order in which the remaining half devolves. It links s.22 to the class provisions: s.24 for Kanthi Perera's children, and ss.25 to 29 for Amali Perera's collaterals.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
provisions.why_relevant: Gives Kanthi Perera's three surviving children, Amali, Anusha and Anuk, the half not taken by the surviving spouse, in equal per capita shares. It also confirms that a child of an earlier marriage takes equally with the children of the later marriage.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: The children and remoter descendants failing, the inheritance of the deceased goes to his father and mother in case they are both alive; but if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half
provisions.why_relevant: Amali Perera died issueless, so descendants fail. This section would have given a surviving parent a share, but both her parents were dead before her, which is what carries the devolution on to s.26.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim but the excerpt stops mid-sentence at 'the surviving parent takes half' and drops the rest of s.25, under which a surviving parent takes half and the brothers and sisters (including half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent) take the other half; s.25 is displaced here only on the researcher's unstated reading that Amali Perera's father died before her.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Father and mother both failing, the property of the intestate goes to his brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or balf-blood, and their children and other issue by representation.
provisions.why_relevant: Both of Amali Perera's parents predeceased her, so the half of her estate not taken by her surviving husband goes to her brothers and sisters. Anusha and Anuk are her half-blood siblings on the mother's side and are expressly included.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus. The corpus body carries the typographical error balf-blood for half-blood; the excerpt is reproduced exactly as it stands in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: In case all the half-brothers and sisters, their children and remoter issue, are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of the inheritance, unless there be a grandfather or grandmother or higher ascendant yet alive, related to the intestate on the other side
provisions.why_relevant: Amali Perera left no full brother or sister; her only siblings were the two half-blood siblings on her mother's side. This section, not the split in s.27, governs and gives them the whole of the collateral half, subject to there being no surviving ascendant on her father's side.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
provisions.why_relevant: Anusha and Anuk are equally near in degree to Amali Perera, so the collateral half is divided between them per capita and not by representation.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.
provisions.verifier_note: Verbatim but the excerpt drops the opening qualifier 'Except when otherwise expressly provided,', which matters because ss.25, 26 and 27 expressly provide for taking by representation.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Save as aforesaid, this Ordinance shall not apply to Kandyans or Muslims, or to Tamils of the Northern Province who are or may become subject to the Tesawalamai.
provisions.why_relevant: Sets the boundary of the Ordinance. The devolution answers hold only if the family is governed by the general law rather than by Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Tesawalamai. Nothing in the scenario suggests any of the three, and the property and the parties are in Colombo.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: The following sections of this Ordinance shall apply to the estates of such persons only as shall die after the proclamation of this Ordinance, and shall be then unmarried or (if married) shall have been married after the proclamation of this Ordinance.
provisions.why_relevant: Confirms that Part III applies to these estates: both Kanthi Perera and Amali Perera died in 2014 and both were married long after the proclamation of the Ordinance.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary

The quoted wording therefore post-dates the matter reference date of April 2019 and all the deeds in the scenario. The underlying requirement of a written, notarially attested deed dates from 1840, but the exact wording relied on here cannot be shown from the corpus to have been in force in 2005, 2013 or 2015. Used as background only.

provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1889; the corpus records a change by Act No. 14 of 1993, before the 2015 conveyance and before the reference date.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Such woman shall, subject and without prejudice to any such trusts as aforesaid, have as full power of disposing of and dealing with such property, by any lawful act inter vivos with the written consent of her husband, but not otherwise, or by last will without such consent, as if she were unmarried.

Because the corpus cannot settle whether the requirement survived into 2005 and 2013, this provision is marked not applicable and is recorded only to flag the point.

provisions.why_relevant: Marks the outer edge of the statutory scheme. Where the Ordinance is silent the answer comes from Roman-Dutch law, which the corpus does not hold. It is the reason the second question cannot be answered from statute alone.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The pedigree is a chain of intestate devolutions of immovable property in Colombo. Every step is fixed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance: the governing law (s.21), the surviving spouse's half (s.22), the order of classes (s.23), the children's half (s.24), the passing over of dead parents (s.25) to brothers and sisters (s.26), the treatment of half-blood siblings related on one side only (s.29) and per capita division (s.30). The intervening deeds are recited facts, not contested questions of law. No judicial authority is needed to draw the pedigree itself.

legal_issues.issue: What property formed part of Kanthi Perera's intestate estate at her death on 1st September 2014, given the 2005 gift of Lot 1 subject to a reserved life interest.
How Kanthi Perera's intestate estate devolves between her surviving husband Kamal De Silva and her three children Amali, Anusha and Anuk.
How Amali Perera's inherited share devolves on her death intestate and issueless about a month later, leaving a surviving husband, no living parent, and two half-blood siblings on her mother's side.
What effect the Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 and Kamal De Silva's subsequent gift of his share to his two children have on the pedigree.

questions.hop_count_basis: Four necessary linked steps: (1) s.21 makes the Ordinance the governing law for the immovable property; (2) s.22 gives the surviving spouse one-half of Kanthi Perera's estate; (3) s.24 divides the other half among the three children, producing Amali Perera's one sixth; (4) that one sixth is then re-devolved on Amali Perera's own intestacy through s.22 read with ss.26, 29 and 30. Only these dependencies are counted; ss.2, 20, 23 and 25 are recorded as supporting.

enrichment.original_background: By a Final Decree dated 2nd December 1999 entered in DC Colombo Partition case No. 523/P, premises bearing Assessment No. 35, Sarasavi Lane Colombo 3 depicted as Lot 3 in Plan No. 2131 dated 12th June 1998 made by Lal Peiris Licensed Surveyor in extent of 30 perches was allotted to Kanthi Perera. She purchased Lot 2 in extent of 30 perches of the said Plan from her brother Wimal Perera by Deed of Transfer 456 dated 6th February 2000 attested Sarath Wickremasinghe Notary Public Colombo. Kanthi Perera amalgamated the said 2 lots and caused to be subdivided into 3 lots depicted as Lot 1,2 and 3 (bearing Assessment Nos. 35/1, 35/2 and 35/3 respectively) in Plan No.567 dated 10th June 2001 made by the same surveyor each containing in extent 20 perches. Mrs Kanthi Perera gifted Lot 1 thereof to Amali Perera a minor who was 16 years old, her daughter from a previous marriage by Deed of Gift No. 1054 dated 6th February 2005 attested by Jagath Perera Notary Public subject to her life interest. In 2013 she sold this property. Mrs Kanthi Perera died intestate on 1st September 2014. Her estate was administered in DC Colombo case No. 567/T and her husband Kamal De Silva was appointed as Administrator. Proceedings of this case was terminated on 6th November 2015. Kanthi had two children out of her marriage to Kamal De Silva namely Anusha and Anuk. Kamal De silva wrote an Administrators Conveyance on 3rd December 2015 and passed the title of Kanthi Perera's intestate Estate to her heirs. Thereafter he gifted his share of the Estate to his two children. Amali Perea was living with his father and after her marriage to Anura Fernando he passed away. Amali met with an accident after one month of her mothers death and died intestate and issueless.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The pedigree has to trace the devolution of Kanthi Perera's intestate estate from her acquisition of the land in 1999 and 2000 down to the present owners. Three questions arise: what remained in her estate at her death on 1st September 2014, how that estate devolved on her surviving husband and her three children, and how Amali Perera's inherited share devolved when she died intestate and issueless about a month later.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21), which applies to the estate of a person who dies after the proclamation of the Ordinance and who was married after it (s.20), and which does not reach Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse inherits one-half (s.22). Subject to that half, the inheritance passes first to descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals (s.23), and children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita (s.24). Where descendants fail, the estate goes to the parents, and only a surviving parent takes a half (s.25); where both parents have failed it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood (s.26). Where all the half-brothers and sisters are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole of that inheritance unless a grandparent or higher ascendant on the other side is alive (s.29), and persons equally near in degree take per capita (s.30).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kanthi Perera became entitled to Lot 3 of Plan No. 2131 by the Final Decree of 2nd December 1999 in DC Colombo case No. 523/P and to Lot 2 of the same plan by Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 6th February 2000, and she amalgamated and resubdivided the two into Lots 1, 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 of 10th June 2001, each 20 perches. By Deed of Gift No. 1054 of 6th February 2005 she gifted Lot 1 to her daughter Amali Perera subject to her own life interest, so from 2005 Lot 1 no longer belonged to her and formed no part of her intestate estate, and her life interest in it ended at her death in any event. Her intestate estate on 1st September 2014 therefore consisted of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567. She left her husband Kamal De Silva surviving, so under s.22 he took one half. Under ss.23 and 24 the other half went in equal per capita shares to her three children, Amali of the earlier marriage and Anusha and Anuk of the marriage to Kamal De Silva, giving each of them one sixth. The Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 in DC Colombo case No. 567/T conveyed the estate to those heirs and records, rather than creates, a devolution that took effect by operation of law at the death. Kamal De Silva then gifted his own one half to Anusha and Anuk, one quarter to each. Amali Perera died intestate and issueless about one month after her mother, leaving her husband Anura Fernando. Under s.22 he takes one half of her one sixth, that is one twelfth. Her descendants having failed and both her parents being dead, her mother on 1st September 2014 and her father after her marriage to Anura Fernando, s.25 gives nothing to a surviving parent and s.26 sends the other one twelfth to her brothers and sisters. Her only siblings are Anusha and Anuk, half blood on her mother's side, and on the footing that no grandparent or higher ascendant on her father's side survived her, s.29 gives them the whole of that share and s.30 divides it between them per capita, one twenty-fourth each.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Kanthi Perera, entitled under the Final Decree of 1999 and Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 2000 and holding Lots 1, 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 from 2001, gifted Lot 1 away in 2005 by Deed of Gift No. 1054 and died intestate on 1st September 2014, whereupon Lots 2 and 3 devolved as to one half on Kamal De Silva and as to one sixth each on Amali Perera, Anusha and Anuk. Amali Perera then died intestate and issueless, her one sixth passing one twelfth to Anura Fernando and one twenty-fourth each to Anusha and Anuk. Kamal De Silva gifted his one half equally to Anusha and Anuk. The present owners are therefore Anusha and Anuk with eleven twenty-fourths each and Anura Fernando with two twenty-fourths, that is one twelfth. This is subject to the family being governed by the general law and to no ascendant of Amali Perera on her father's side having survived her; the scenario states neither expressly.

answer_claims.claim_text: Inheritance ab intestato to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a deceased person is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, which applies to persons dying after its proclamation who were married after it and which does not extend to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, inheritance passes first to descendants, and children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita.
Where the descendants fail and both parents of the intestate are dead, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the intestate, whether of the whole or half blood.

Where all the half-brothers and sisters are related to the intestate on one side only they take the whole of that inheritance, unless a grandparent or higher ascendant on the other side is alive, and those equally near in degree take per capita.

Kanthi Perera's intestate estate consisted of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567, because Lot 1 had passed to Amali Perera by Deed of Gift No. 1054 of 2005 and Kanthi Perera's reserved life interest in it ended at her death.
On Kanthi Perera's death intestate on 1st September 2014 her surviving husband Kamal De Silva took one half of Lots 2 and 3.
The remaining half went in equal shares to Kanthi Perera's three children Amali, Anusha and Anuk, so each took one sixth of Lots 2 and 3.

The Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 in DC Colombo case No. 567/T conveyed the estate to those heirs and records a devolution that had already taken effect by operation of law at the death.
Amali Perera died intestate and issueless about one month after her mother, leaving her husband Anura Fernando, who took one half of her one sixth, namely one twelfth of Lots 2 and 3.

Both of Amali Perera's parents having predeceased her and her only siblings being Anusha and Anuk of the half blood on her mother's side, and on the footing that no ascendant on her father's side survived her, the other one twelfth went to Anusha and Anuk per capita, one twenty-fourth each.
Kamal De Silva gifted the one half he had inherited to his two children Anusha and Anuk, giving each of them a further one quarter.
The pedigree ends with Anusha and Anuk holding eleven twenty-fourths each and Anura Fernando holding one twelfth of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The two clearest instances turn on rules the corpus does not hold. First, the gift of Lot 1 to Amali Perera when she was sixteen requires a rule on the capacity of a minor donee and on acceptance of a donation through a parent or guardian; the Age of Majority Ordinance is absent from the corpus and the acceptance rule is Roman-Dutch, to which the Ordinance itself defers by s.36. Second, the 2013 sale of Lot 1 turns on what a life tenant can pass and therefore on whether the owner of the property subject to the life interest had to join, and the corpus contains no provision on reserved life interests. A third candidate, the Administrator's Conveyance executed after the testamentary proceedings had been terminated, is only partly reached by Civil Procedure Code s.542. A complete answer needs non-statutory authority, so the question cannot be proposed as statute-only gold.

Whether the 2013 sale of Lot 1 required the owner of the property subject to the reserved life interest to join in the deed, the seller holding only a life interest.
Whether the Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 required a further step in DC Colombo case No. 567/T, the proceedings having been terminated on 6th November 2015.
Whether the written consent of Kanthi Perera's husband was required for her 2005 gift and for the 2013 sale of her separate immovable property.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether any of the deeds in the pedigree could have been validly executed only with a further step or with another party joining, and if so which two instances best illustrate the point.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Not settled on the corpus. The Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 requires a notarially attested deed for any disposition of immovable property, but the text in the corpus is the post-2022 consolidation and its express rule that a guardian may act for a minor transferee comes from later amendment. Civil Procedure Code s.530 requires steps to be taken to appoint a guardian or manager where an heir or beneficiary in a testamentary case is a minor, and s.585 provides for a certificate of curatorship over a minor's property. Civil Procedure Code s.542 fixes the reach and duration of an administrator's power. Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.8, on the corpus text, requires the written consent of the husband for an inter vivos disposition by a married woman of her separate immovable property, and s.36 sends whatever the Ordinance does not cover to Roman-Dutch law.
gold_answer_draft.application: The strongest candidate instances are, first, Deed of Gift No. 1054 of 6th February 2005, where the donee Amali Perera was sixteen, so acceptance of the gift would have had to be made on her behalf by a parent or guardian; and second, the 2013 sale of Lot 1, where the seller held only the life interest reserved by the 2005 gift, so the owner of the property subject to that interest would have had to join the deed for a full title to pass. A third candidate is the Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015, written after the proceedings in DC Colombo case No. 567/T had been terminated on 6th November 2015, which raises whether a further application to the District Court was needed before the administrator could convey. A fourth is the written consent of Kanthi Perera's husband to her 2005 gift and to the 2013 sale, if the requirement in the corpus text of s.8 was still in force. None of these can be carried through on the corpus alone: the age at which Amali Perera ceased to be a minor is not fixed by any general provision in the corpus, the rule on acceptance for a minor donee is Roman-Dutch, no provision in the corpus governs a reserved life interest, and the corpus does not say whether an administrator may convey after termination of the proceedings.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Reserved. Two instances can be identified with some confidence as a matter of conveyancing practice, the acceptance of the 2005 gift on behalf of the minor donee and the joining of the owner subject to the life interest in the 2013 sale, but neither can be grounded in a provision of the frozen corpus that was in force at the relevant time, so no statute-only gold answer is proposed.

answer_claims.claim_text: Every disposition of immovable property in the pedigree had to be by a deed executed before and attested by a notary, so any missing party or missing step goes to the validity of the deed itself.
Where the Ordinance is silent on a question of intestate distribution the rules of Roman-Dutch law govern, and the corpus does not hold those rules.

The corpus provides for a guardian or manager to be appointed where a beneficiary in a testamentary case is a minor and for a certificate of curatorship over a minor's property, but neither provision reaches the acceptance of a deed of gift by a minor donee outside those proceedings.

The Administrator's Conveyance of 3rd December 2015 was executed after the testamentary proceedings had been terminated on 6th November 2015, and the only provision in the corpus that bears on the point fixes the reach and duration of the power of administration without saying whether a conveyance may follow termination.

Whether Kanthi Perera needed her husband's written consent for the 2005 gift and the 2013 sale cannot be settled, because the corpus text still carries the consent requirement while recording no amendment history for the section.
No statute-only answer is proposed for this question, because each candidate instance depends on authority outside the frozen corpus or on wording that post-dates the deed in question.

questions.block_reason: A complete answer needs non-statutory authority. The capacity of a sixteen-year-old donee and acceptance of a gift on her behalf rest on the Age of Majority Ordinance, which is not in the corpus, and on Roman-Dutch donation rules to which Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.36 defers. The joining of the owner subject to a reserved life interest in the 2013 sale has no statutory basis in the corpus. The only corpus provision naming a guardian as competent to act for a minor transferee, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(2)(b), comes from an amendment made after the matter reference date and long after the 2005 deed. Verifier: the s.8 consent point is unresolved rather than merely unlikely, because the corpus holds no repealing or amending instrument for s.8 and the related s.11 dispensation procedure was not recorded; the question stays reserved.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The present shares are the arithmetic result of two intestate devolutions plus one recited gift. Each fraction comes from a provision of Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance: s.22 for the spouse's half on each death, s.24 for the equal shares of the children, and ss.26, 29 and 30 for the half-blood siblings on Amali Perera's intestacy. The gift by Kamal De Silva of his own inherited half is a recited fact, not a question of law.

legal_issues.issue: What fractions of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 each heir took on Kanthi Perera's intestacy.
How Amali Perera's one sixth was redistributed on her own intestacy between her surviving husband and her half-blood siblings.
What each heir owns today once Kamal De Silva's gift of his inherited half to Anusha and Anuk is taken into account.

questions.hop_count_basis: Four necessary linked steps, the same chain as the pedigree question carried through to fractions: s.22 for Kamal De Silva's half, s.24 for the one sixth each of the three children, s.22 again for Anura Fernando's half of Amali Perera's share, and s.26 read with ss.29 and 30 for the one twenty-fourth each taken by Anusha and Anuk out of Amali Perera's estate. Verifier: PROV-M087-001 (s.21) moved from supporting to indispensable so that the gateway provision carries the same role it has in M087-Q01; it is the first of the four steps and adds no further hop.

enrichment.original_background: By a Final Decree dated 2nd December 1999 entered in DC Colombo Partition case No. 523/P, premises bearing Assessment No. 35, Sarasavi Lane Colombo 3 depicted as Lot 3 in Plan No. 2131 dated 12th June 1998 made by Lal Peiris Licensed Surveyor in extent of 30 perches was allotted to Kanthi Perera. She purchased Lot 2 in extent of 30 perches of the said Plan from her brother Wimal Perera by Deed of Transfer 456 dated 6th February 2000 attested Sarath Wickremasinghe Notary Public Colombo. Kanthi Perera amalgamated the said 2 lots and caused to be subdivided into 3 lots depicted as Lot 1,2 and 3 (bearing Assessment Nos. 35/1, 35/2 and 35/3 respectively) in Plan No.567 dated 10th June 2001 made by the same surveyor each containing in extent 20 perches. Mrs Kanthi Perera gifted Lot 1 thereof to Amali Perera a minor who was 16 years old, her daughter from a previous marriage by Deed of Gift No. 1054 dated 6th February 2005 attested by Jagath Perera Notary Public subject to her life interest. In 2013 she sold this property. Mrs Kanthi Perera died intestate on 1st September 2014. Her estate was administered in DC Colombo case No. 567/T and her husband Kamal De Silva was appointed as Administrator. Proceedings of this case was terminated on 6th November 2015. Kanthi had two children out of her marriage to Kamal De Silva namely Anusha and Anuk. Kamal De silva wrote an Administrators Conveyance on 3rd December 2015 and passed the title of Kanthi Perera's intestate Estate to her heirs. Thereafter he gifted his share of the Estate to his two children. Amali Perea was living with his father and after her marriage to Anura Fernando he passed away. Amali met with an accident after one month of her mothers death and died intestate and issueless.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What share of the property each heir presently owns. The property in question is Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567, which is what remained of Kanthi Perera's holding after Lot 1 had been gifted away in 2005 and disposed of in 2013.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of an intestate (Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.22). Subject to that half, descendants come first and children take equally per capita (ss.23 and 24). Where descendants fail and both parents are dead, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the intestate whether of the whole or half blood (ss.25 and 26); where all the half-blood siblings are related on one side only they take the whole of that share unless an ascendant on the other side survives (s.29), and persons equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). Inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by these provisions (s.21), which apply to these estates (ss.2 and 20).
gold_answer_draft.application: On Kanthi Perera's death intestate on 1st September 2014, Kamal De Silva took one half of Lots 2 and 3 as surviving spouse, and Amali, Anusha and Anuk took the other half in equal shares, one sixth each. Amali Perera died about a month later, intestate and issueless, leaving her husband Anura Fernando; he took one half of her one sixth, that is one twelfth. Her descendants having failed and both her parents being dead, the other one twelfth passed to her brother and sister of the half blood on her mother's side, Anusha and Anuk, per capita, one twenty-fourth each, on the footing that no ascendant on her father's side survived her. Kamal De Silva then gifted the one half he had inherited to Anusha and Anuk, one quarter to each. Adding the three sources for each of them, Anusha holds one quarter by gift, one sixth by inheritance from her mother and one twenty-fourth from Amali Perera, that is six, four and one twenty-fourths, or eleven twenty-fourths; Anuk holds the same eleven twenty-fourths; and Anura Fernando holds two twenty-fourths. The three shares total twenty-four twenty-fourths.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567, Anusha owns eleven twenty-fourths, Anuk owns eleven twenty-fourths and Anura Fernando owns one twelfth, that is two twenty-fourths. Kamal De Silva retains nothing, having gifted his half away. These shares assume the family is governed by the general law and that no ascendant of Amali Perera on her father's side survived her. Lot 1 is left out of account because it had been gifted to Amali Perera in 2005 and the scenario states that it was sold in 2013; the scenario does not make clear who sold it, and if only the reserved life interest was in fact sold, Lot 1 would have fallen into Amali Perera's estate and would now be held one half by Anura Fernando and one quarter each by Anusha and Anuk.

answer_claims.claim_text: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person dying intestate.
Subject to the spouse's half, the children of the intestate are preferent to all others and take equally per capita.

Where descendants fail and both parents are dead the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the whole or half blood, half-blood siblings related on one side only take the whole of that share absent an ascendant on the other side, and those equally near in degree take per capita.
On Kanthi Perera's intestacy Kamal De Silva took one half of Lots 2 and 3 and Amali, Anusha and Anuk took one sixth each.
Amali Perera's one sixth devolved one twelfth on her husband Anura Fernando and one twenty-fourth on each of Anusha and Anuk.
Kamal De Silva's gift of his inherited half to Anusha and Anuk added one quarter to each of them.
Anusha and Anuk each presently own eleven twenty-fourths of Lots 2 and 3 of Plan No. 567 and Anura Fernando owns one twelfth, Kamal De Silva retaining nothing.
